docs.title: liveplot
docs.text: Live training curves in Jupyter, Colab and the VS Code / Cursor interactive window, with a tqdm bar underneath, at (almost) no cost to the training loop.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install "liveplot[notebook] @ git+https://github.com/ARENA-education/liveplot.git"

matplotlib, numpy and pillow are the requirements. The notebook extra adds ipython for the live display and tqdm for the progress bar. A notebook already has both, so plain pip install git+https://github.com/ARENA-education/liveplot.git is enough there.

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text:
from liveplot import LivePlot

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss | acc", "lr")   # wrap the loop, like tqdm
plot["acc"].set_ylim(0, 1)                    # configure, like matplotlib
for batch in plot:
    loss, acc = train_step(batch)
    plot.log(loss=loss, acc=acc, lr=lr)       # log, like wandb
  • Wrap the loop. LivePlot(loader) yields the loader's items. Each item moves the x-axis one step and updates the progress bar. plot.log on its own does not move x.
  • Log by name. plot.log(loss=loss) adds a point to the curve loss at the current x. A metric exists from the first time you log it.
  • Lay out with strings. Each string is one panel. Names separated by spaces share a y-axis. Names after | go on a right-hand y-axis. Here loss and acc share a panel with two y-axes, and lr has its own panel. With no strings, every metric shares one panel.
  • Configure with matplotlib's names. plot["acc"] is the y-axis that holds acc.

For nested epoch and batch loops, create the plot once and wrap the inner loop with plot(...). The x-axis continues across epochs:

plot = LivePlot("loss", "acc")
for epoch in range(epochs):
    for batch in plot(loader, desc=f"epoch {epoch}"):
        plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))      # one point per batch
    plot.log(acc=evaluate())                  # one point per epoch
plot.finish()

The plot is drawn by a separate process and shown as a plain image, so it behaves the same in every notebook front end, and interrupting a cell is safe. Everything you log is also kept in plot.data.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
This page is generated from the docstrings in liveplot/liveplot.py.

The library has one public class, LivePlot. Its panels and axes are small handle objects that you get from the plot:

Object How to get it LivePlot LivePlot(...) or LivePlot.subplots(...) Panel plot.panels[i], plot[metric].panel, or the second value returned by LivePlot.subplots Axis plot[metric], panel.left, panel.right, panel.twinx()

docs.title: LivePlot
docs.text:
LivePlot(
    *args,
    total: int | None = None,
    initial: int | float = 0,
    unit: str = "step",
    unit_scale: int | float = 1,
    refresh_seconds: float = 1.0,
    max_cols: int | None = 3,
    rows: int | None = None,
    cols: int | None = None,
    cell_size: tuple = (5, 3.5),
    dpi: int = 100,
    show: bool = True,
    progress: bool = True,
    desc: str | None = None,
    record: bool | str = False,
    smooth: float | None = None,
    fixed_x: bool = False,
)

A live plot of the metrics you log, with a tqdm progress bar underneath.

Metrics are named when you log them: plot.log(loss=0.3). Each name becomes a curve, and the figure redraws in the notebook's output cell while the loop runs.

The x value of a point is the plot's step counter at the time of the log call. log itself does not advance the counter. Advance it in one of three ways:

  1. Iterate the plot: for batch in LivePlot(loader). Each item advances the counter by one.
  2. Wrap an inner loop with plot(loader), or call plot.update() once per step. Use these for nested epoch and batch loops.
  3. Pass the x value yourself: plot.log(step, loss=0.3).

If you do none of these, every point is logged at the same x (initial, 0 by default) and the curve collapses to a vertical line.

Outside a notebook nothing is drawn, but data still collects everything.

Example 
from liveplot import LivePlot

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss | acc", "lr")   # two panels; acc on a right-hand axis
plot["acc"].set_ylim(0, 1)
for batch in plot:                            # wrapping the loader advances x
    loss, acc = train_step(batch)
    plot.log(loss=loss, acc=acc, lr=get_lr())

The refresh_seconds argument.

The default smoothing weight for panels.

"process" when a separate render process draws the figure, "thread" when that process could not start or died, and drawing happens inside log, "off" when nothing is drawn (show=False, or not in a notebook, and not recording).

The plot-wide vertical lines added with axvline.

Create a plot: LivePlot([iterable,] *panels, **options).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default *args Any

An optional iterable, then any number of panel layouts.

The iterable is anything you would loop over: a range, a DataLoader, an existing tqdm bar. If the first argument is not a string or a dict, it is taken as the iterable. Iterating the plot then yields its items, advances x by one per item, shows a progress bar, and calls finish() when the loop ends. An existing tqdm bar is reused, not wrapped in a second one. Leave the iterable out for nested loops and use plot(inner_iterable) or plot.update().

Each layout string is one panel. Names separated by spaces share the left y-axis. Names after a | go on a right-hand y-axis: "loss", "train_loss val_loss", "loss | acc". With no layout, every metric you log shares one panel. With a layout, a metric that no string mentions gets a panel of its own. A dict such as {"metrics": ["acc"], "ylim": (0, 1)} is also accepted in place of a string, but the setters are the intended way to configure a panel.

() total int | None

Number of items in the whole run. Optional. Defaults to len(iterable) when there is an iterable with a length. It does two things. It is the length of the progress bar when the bar cannot get one from the iterable: the bar that update() opens, and the bar for an iterable that has no len(). And with fixed_x=True it fixes the x range. With the default fixed_x=False it does not change the figure. Bars made by plot(iterable) use len(iterable).

None initial int | float

The x value of the first item. Use initial=1 for a 1-based x-axis.

0 unit str

Name of one item. It is the default x label and the unit on the progress bar.

'step' unit_scale int | float

How much x advances per item. x = initial + n * unit_scale. For example unit="examples", unit_scale=batch_size plots against examples seen.

1 refresh_seconds float

Minimum time between redraws. Points that arrive in between are drawn together in the next frame. 0 redraws whenever new data arrives.

1.0 max_cols int | None

Widest grid of panels. None gives a near-square grid.

3 rows int | None

Fix the number of grid rows.

None cols int | None

Fix the number of grid columns.

None cell_size tuple

(width, height) of one panel, in inches.

(5, 3.5) dpi int

Resolution of the rendered image.

100 show bool

False draws nothing. Metrics are still collected in data and shown on the progress bar.

True progress bool

False shows no progress bar.

True desc str | None

Text before the progress bar, for the bar made by iterating the plot or by update(). Bars made by plot(iterable, desc=...) take their own.

None record bool | str

True keeps every rendered frame in frames. A path such as "run.gif" also writes an animated GIF there at finish(). Recording works outside a notebook too.

False smooth float | None

Default smoothing weight for every panel, from 0 up to but not including 1. See set_smooth.

None fixed_x bool

False (the default) lets the x-axis grow with the data. True, with a known total, fixes the x-axis to (initial, initial + total * unit_scale) from the first frame, so the curve grows into an axis that already spans the run. It has no effect without a total.

False

docs.title: panels property
docs.text:
panels: list

The panels of the grid, in order, as a list of Panel.

Example 
plot.panels[0].set_title("training")

docs.title: x_range property
docs.text:
x_range

The fixed x-axis range, or None when the x-axis follows the data.

It is (initial, initial + total * unit_scale) when fixed_x=True and total is known, and None otherwise.

docs.title: step property
docs.text:
step

The x value that a log() call without an explicit step gets right now.

Once a loop is wrapped or update() has been called, this is initial + n * unit_scale. Before that, it is the step of the last log(step, ...) call, or initial if there has been none.

docs.title: subplots classmethod
docs.text:
subplots(
    nrows: int = 1,
    ncols: int = 1,
    *,
    figsize=None,
    squeeze: bool = True,
    width_ratios=None,
    height_ratios=None,
    iterable=None,
    **kwargs,
)

Create a plot with a fixed grid of empty panels, like plt.subplots.

Fill each panel with ax.plot("loss", ...) for curves or ax.imshow(tensor) for an image. The grid never grows: a metric you log without placing it joins the first panel that is still empty, or the first curve panel if none is empty.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default nrows int

Number of grid rows.

1 ncols int

Number of grid columns.

1 figsize tuple[float, float] | None

(width, height) of the whole figure in inches. Without it, each panel is cell_size inches.

None squeeze bool

True returns one Panel for a 1x1 grid, a flat list for a single row or column, and a 2-d grid otherwise. False always returns the 2-d grid.

True width_ratios Sequence[float] | None

Relative column widths, one per column, e.g. (1, 1.3).

None height_ratios Sequence[float] | None

Relative row heights, one per row.

None iterable Iterable | None

An iterable to wrap, as in LivePlot(iterable).

None **kwargs Any

Any other LivePlot option, such as total or smooth.

{}

Returns:

Type Description tuple[LivePlot, Panel | list[Panel] | _PanelGrid]

(plot, axes), the plot and its panels.

Example 
plot, (ax_loss, ax_samples) = LivePlot.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
ax_loss.plot("lossD", "lossG")           # two metrics on the left axis
ax_loss.twinx().plot("D_real")           # one on the right-hand axis
for batch in plot(loader):
    plot.log(lossD=..., lossG=..., D_real=...)
    if plot.n % 250 == 0:
        ax_samples.imshow(netG(fixed_noise), rows=2, vmin=-1, vmax=1)
plot.finish()

docs.title: __call__
docs.text:
__call__(iterable, **tqdm_kwargs)

Wrap a loop so that each item advances the x-axis by one step: plot(loader).

Use this for nested loops. Create the plot once, then wrap the inner loop on every epoch. The step count continues from one wrapped loop to the next, and each gets its own progress bar of length len(iterable). The count is 0 inside the body for the first item, like for step in range(n). The plot is not finished when the loop ends, so call finish() yourself or use with.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default iterable Iterable

What to loop over. An existing tqdm bar is reused.

required **tqdm_kwargs Any

Passed to tqdm, e.g. desc="epoch 3".

{}

Yields:

Type Description Any

The items of iterable.

Example 
plot = LivePlot("loss", "acc")
for epoch in range(epochs):
    for batch in plot(loader, desc=f"epoch {epoch}"):
        plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))     # one point per batch
    plot.log(acc=evaluate())                 # one point per epoch
plot.finish()

docs.title: update
docs.text:
update(n=1)

Advance the x-axis by hand, like tqdm's update.

Use this when you do not want to wrap the loop. Call it once per step, after logging that step's metrics. The first call opens one progress bar for the whole run, of length total if you gave one, and finish() closes it.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default n int

How many items to advance by.

1 Example 
plot = LivePlot(total=epochs * len(loader))   # total only sets the bar's length
for epoch in range(epochs):
    plot.set_description(f"epoch {epoch}")
    for batch in loader:
        plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))
        plot.update()
plot.finish()

docs.title: __iter__
docs.text:
__iter__()

Iterate over the iterable given to the constructor: for batch in plot.

Each item advances the x-axis by one step, a progress bar is shown, and finish() is called when the loop ends, including when it ends with break or an exception. Raises TypeError if the plot was created without an iterable.

docs.title: log
docs.text:
log(*args, **metrics)

Record one value for each of one or more metrics.

A metric is created the first time you log it. Each call adds one point per metric, at the plot's current x (plot.step). Metrics can be logged at different rates: each keeps its own list of points.

log does not advance x. Wrap the loop (for batch in plot or plot(loader)), call plot.update(), or pass the step as the first argument. Otherwise every point has the same x.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default *args Any

Optionally the x value for this call, then optionally a dict of metrics: log(step, loss=0.3), log(step, {"loss": 0.3}) or log({"loss": 0.3}). In a wrapped loop an explicit step applies to this call only. With no wrapped loop it also becomes the x of later calls that give no step.

() **metrics float

Metric values by name: log(loss=0.3, acc=0.9). A value is anything float() accepts, including a one-element tensor.

{} Example 
plot = LivePlot(range(1000), "loss | acc")
for step in plot:
    plot.log(loss=train_step())      # every step
    if step % 50 == 0:
        plot.log(acc=evaluate())     # every 50 steps, same x-axis

docs.title: axhline
docs.text:
axhline(y, label=None, *, metric=None, **kwargs)

Draw a horizontal reference line.

With metric, the line goes on the axis that holds that metric, the same as plot[metric].axhline(y, label). Without it, the line goes on the left axis of every panel that exists now. Panels created later do not get it. The line is dashed grey by default and has a legend entry.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default y float

Where to draw the line.

required label str | None

The legend text. Defaults to the value of y.

None metric str | None

Draw the line only on the axis holding this metric.

None **kwargs Any

Passed to matplotlib's Axes.axhline (color, linestyle, linewidth, alpha, ...).

{} Example 
plot.axhline(math.log(d_vocab), "uniform", metric="loss")

docs.title: axvline
docs.text:
axvline(x=None, label=None, **kwargs)

Draw a vertical line on every curve panel, including panels created later.

The line is dotted grey by default. For one panel only, use Panel.axvline.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x float | None

Where to draw the line. Defaults to the current step (plot.step) at the time of the call.

None label str | None

Text written along the line. It does not go in the legend.

None **kwargs Any

Passed to matplotlib's Axes.axvline (color, linestyle, ...).

{} Example 
if step == warmup_steps:
    plot.axvline(label="warmup ends")

docs.title: imshow
docs.text:
imshow(x, **kwargs)

Show an image, or a batch of images as a grid, replacing the previous one.

The picture goes on the plot's first image panel. If the plot has none, one is added. On a plot made by subplots, an image panel must already exist, so call imshow on a panel there first.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x ArrayLike

A torch tensor, numpy array or other array-like. See Panel.imshow for the accepted shapes.

required **kwargs Any

Passed to Panel.imshow (rows, cols, vmin, vmax, ...).

{}

Returns:

Type Description Panel

The panel that holds the image.

Example 
plot = LivePlot(range(steps))
for step in plot:
    plot.log(loss=train_step())
    if step % 100 == 0:
        plot.imshow(model(holdout), vmin=0, vmax=1)

docs.title: figure
docs.text:
figure()

Build a matplotlib Figure of the plot as it stands.

The figure has the same panels, data, reference lines and images as the live plot. It is built from data on the calling thread and is separate from the live display, so changing it does not change the live plot. It works during or after the run, and also with show=False or outside a notebook.

Returns:

Type Description Figure

A new figure.

Example 
fig = plot.figure()
fig.suptitle("run 12")
fig.savefig("run12.png", dpi=150)

docs.title: refresh
docs.text:
refresh()

Redraw now, if drawing happens on the calling thread (mode == "thread").

In the usual mode a separate process draws on its own schedule and this does nothing.

docs.title: finish
docs.text:
finish()

Draw the final frame, close the progress bar and stop the render process.

Iterating the plot (for batch in plot) and the with block call this for you. Call it yourself after nested loops that use plot(loader) or plot.update(). Calling it twice is safe. data stays available afterwards. If record was a path, the GIF is written here.

docs.title: __enter__
docs.text:
__enter__()

Use the plot as a context manager: finish() is called when the block exits.

Example 
with LivePlot("loss") as plot:
    for step in range(num_steps):
        plot.log(step, loss=train_step())

docs.title: Panel
docs.text:
Panel(plot, index: int)

One panel of the grid: a set of curves with one or two y-axes, or one image.

You do not create these. Get one from plot.panels[i], from plot[metric].panel, or from LivePlot.subplots, which returns the panels of a fixed grid.

A panel has a title, an x-axis, a legend and a smoothing weight, and up to two y-axes: panel.left and panel.right. The y setters on the panel itself (set_ylabel, set_ylim, set_yscale, axhline) act on the left axis.

Setters can be called before the loop or during it. The figure is laid out again on the next frame.

Example 
plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss | acc", "lr")
plot.panels[0].set_title("training")
plot.panels[0].right.set_ylim(0, 1)   # the axis holding acc
plot.panels[1].set_yscale("log")      # the lr panel

docs.title: imshow
docs.text:
imshow(
    x,
    *,
    rows=None,
    cols=None,
    griddim=None,
    vmin=None,
    vmax=None,
    scale_each=False,
    channels=None,
    cmap="gray",
    padding=0,
    pad_value=0,
    max_images=64,
    max_cols=8,
)

Show an image, or a batch of images as a grid, on this panel.

Each call replaces the previous picture. Once the plot has a step (a loop is wrapped or something has been logged), the panel's title shows the step the picture was drawn at.

Accepted shapes: (H, W), (1, H, W), (H, W, 3|4), (B, H, W), (B, 1|3|4, H, W) and (B, H, W, 1|3|4). (3, H, W) and (4, H, W) are ambiguous and raise ValueError; pass channels. A 3-d array whose last dimension is 3 or 4 is read as one colour image.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default x ArrayLike

A torch tensor, numpy array, or anything numpy.asarray accepts. Tensors are detached and moved to the CPU for you.

required rows int | None

Number of grid rows. The number of columns is inferred.

None cols int | None

Number of grid columns. The number of rows is inferred.

None griddim tuple[int, int] | None

(rows, cols), fixing both. Missing cells are left blank and extra images are dropped. Do not combine with rows or cols.

None vmin float | None

Value at the dark end of the range. Defaults to the minimum of the batch.

None vmax float | None

Value at the bright end of the range. Defaults to the maximum of the batch. Fixing vmin and vmax stops the brightness changing from frame to frame. They apply to colour images too. uint8 input is shown as it is unless one of them is given.

None scale_each bool

Scale each image to its own range instead of the batch's.

False channels str | None

How to read a 3-d input: "first" for (C, H, W), "last" for (H, W, C), "none" for a batch of grayscale (B, H, W).

None cmap str

Matplotlib colormap for grayscale images.

'gray' padding int

Pixels of pad_value around every image in a grid. 0 puts them edge to edge.

0 pad_value int

The value (0 to 255) of padding pixels and blank cells.

0 max_images int | None

docs.title: Is total needed? What does it change?
docs.text:
No. You can leave it out.

total is the number of items in the whole run, with the same meaning as tqdm's total. It does two things:

  • It sets the length of the progress bar when the bar cannot work it out: the bar that plot.update() opens, and the bar for an iterable that has no len(). With a length, the bar shows a percentage and a time remaining.
  • With fixed_x=True, it fixes the x-axis to the whole run from the first frame.

fixed_x is False by default. The x-axis then grows with the data, and the figure looks the same with or without total.

If you wrap something that has a length, such as LivePlot(loader) or LivePlot(range(n)), total is taken from len(). Bars made by plot(loader) always use len(loader) and ignore total.

See The x-axis and total.

docs.title: Why wrap the dataloader?
docs.text:
Because wrapping is what moves the x-axis. LivePlot(loader) and plot(loader) count the items they yield, and that count is the x value of every point you log.

plot.log records values. It does not advance x. If nothing advances x, every point is logged at x = 0 and you get a vertical line instead of a curve:

plot = LivePlot()
for batch in loader:
    plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))   # every point at x = 0

There are three ways to advance x. Use whichever fits your loop.

# 1. Wrap the loop
plot = LivePlot("loss")
for batch in plot(loader):
    plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))
plot.finish()

# 2. Call update() once per step
plot = LivePlot("loss")
for batch in loader:
    plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))
    plot.update()
plot.finish()

# 3. Pass the step yourself
plot = LivePlot("loss")
for step, batch in enumerate(loader):
    plot.log(step, loss=train_step(batch))
plot.finish()

Wrapping also gives you the progress bar. See The x-axis and total.

docs.title: How do I put two metrics on one axis?
docs.text:
Put both names in one layout string, separated by a space:

plot = LivePlot(loader, "train_loss val_loss")

They share a panel and a y-axis, and the legend tells them apart. With no layout strings at all, every metric you log shares one panel.

docs.title: How do I put a metric on the right-hand axis?
docs.text:
Put its name after a |:

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss | acc")
plot["acc"].set_ylim(0, 1)     # plot["acc"] is the right-hand axis

loss uses the left y-axis and acc the right one. Each side can hold several names: "lossD lossG | acc".

docs.title: How do I get several panels?
docs.text:
Give one string per panel:

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss", "acc", "lr")                  # three panels
plot = LivePlot(loader, "train_loss val_loss | acc", "lr")    # two panels, the first with two y-axes

A metric you log that no string mentions gets a panel of its own. See Panels and layout strings.

docs.title: Why is nothing drawn?
docs.text: The live plot only appears in a notebook: Jupyter, Colab, or the VS Code / Cursor interactive window. In a plain script nothing is drawn and no message is shown. The metrics are still collected in plot.data, and plot.figure() still returns a figure you can save.

docs.title: Do I need to call finish()?
docs.text: Not when you iterate the plot itself (for batch in plot) or use with LivePlot(...) as plot:. Both finish the plot for you. Call plot.finish() yourself after loops that use plot(loader) or plot.update(). It draws the last frame, closes the progress bar and stops the render process.

docs.title: Customising axes
docs.text: Titles, labels, limits and scales are set with matplotlib's method names. You can call the setters before the loop or during it. The figure is laid out again on the next frame.

docs.title: Which object to call
docs.text:
Object How to get it What its setters change An axis plot["acc"] One y-axis: the one holding that metric, left or right A panel plot.panels[0], plot["acc"].panel One panel, and its left y-axis The plot plot Every panel, including panels created later 
plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss | acc", "lr")

plot["acc"].set_ylim(0, 1)                   # the right-hand axis of the first panel
plot["acc"].set_ylabel("test accuracy")
plot["lr"].set_yscale("log")

plot.panels[0].set_title("training")         # one panel
plot.panels[0].set_xlim(0, 10_000)

plot.set_xlabel("batches")                   # every panel

plot[metric] finds the axis whichever side it is on, so a right-hand axis needs no special spelling. plot.panels[i].left and plot.panels[i].right name a panel's two axes directly.

docs.title: The setters
docs.text:
On an axis (reference):

Setter Effect set_ylabel(text) The y label set_ylim(low, high) Fix the y range. Also accepts one (low, high) pair. Both limits are required. set_yscale("log") "linear" or "log" axhline(y, label) A horizontal reference line

On a panel (reference):

Setter Effect set_title(text) The title set_xlabel(text) The x label set_xlim(low, high) Fix the x range set_smooth(weight) Smoothing for the panel's curves legend(**kwargs) Move or restyle the legend. The keyword arguments go to matplotlib's Axes.legend. axvline(x, label) A vertical reference line

The panel setters are also available on an axis, where they act on the axis's panel. So plot["acc"].set_title("evaluation") works. The y setters are also available on a panel, where they act on the left axis.

On the plot, set_title, set_xlabel, set_xlim, set_ylabel, set_ylim, set_yscale and set_smooth apply to every panel. The y setters reach left axes only.

docs.title: Several settings at once
docs.text:
set(**kwargs) calls several setters in one go, like matplotlib's Axes.set. Each keyword name=value calls set_name(value):

plot["acc"].set(ylabel="test accuracy", ylim=(0, 1))
plot.panels[0].set(title="training", xlabel="examples")
plot.set(xlabel="examples", smooth=0.9)       # every panel

docs.title: Moving the legend
docs.text:
plot.panels[0].legend(loc="upper left")
plot.panels[0].legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.15), ncols=3)   # under the panel

docs.title: Limits and scales that liveplot does not support
docs.text: set_ylim and set_xlim need both limits. set_yscale accepts "linear" and "log" only. For anything else, build a matplotlib figure with plot.figure() and change it there.

docs.title: A separate render process
docs.text:
plot.log only appends numbers to lists and puts them on a queue. It does no drawing.

A separate process owns the matplotlib figure. It redraws at most once every refresh_seconds (1.0 by default), and only when new data has arrived. Points that arrive between redraws are drawn together in the next frame. refresh_seconds=0 redraws whenever new data arrives, as fast as rendering allows.

Each frame comes back as PNG bytes and replaces the image in the notebook's output cell. The output is a plain image. It needs no widgets and no JavaScript, so it behaves the same in Jupyter, Colab, VS Code and Cursor.

A small background thread shows each frame as soon as it is ready, so a loop that logs rarely still sees its frames on time.

If the render process cannot start, liveplot warns and draws inside log instead. plot.mode tells you which is in use: "process", "thread", or "off" when nothing is drawn.

docs.title: The progress bar
docs.text: The bar is tqdm's (tqdm.auto), shown under the plot. Its postfix shows the latest value of each metric. Pass an existing tqdm bar as the iterable to use yours instead. progress=False turns the bar off.

docs.title: Interrupting a cell
docs.text:
Interrupting is safe. Jupyter sends the interrupt to every process the kernel started, and the render process ignores it. You are left with the last frame, and plot.data holds everything logged so far. Running the cell again starts a new plot.

A plot that is dropped without finish() stops its render process when it is garbage collected. The render process also exits on its own if the notebook kernel dies.

docs.title: Outside a notebook
docs.text: In a plain script nothing is drawn, and no message is shown. plot.data and plot.latest are still filled in, the progress bar still works, and plot.figure() and recording still work.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text: import liveplot imports nothing heavy. matplotlib, numpy and pillow are imported when they are first needed. IPython and tqdm are optional: without IPython nothing is displayed, and without tqdm there is no progress bar.

docs.title: Images with subplots and imshow
docs.text: A panel can hold a picture instead of curves. That lets one figure show loss curves that update every step next to generated samples that update now and then.

docs.title: LivePlot.subplots
docs.text:
LivePlot.subplots follows plt.subplots. It returns the plot and a fixed grid of empty panels. You then say what each panel holds.

plot, (ax_loss, ax_samples) = LivePlot.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4))
ax_loss.plot("lossD", "lossG")            # these metrics go on this panel's left axis
ax_loss.twinx().plot("D_real")            # this one goes on its right-hand axis
ax_samples.set_title("generator samples")

for epoch in range(epochs):
    for imgs, _ in plot(loader, desc=f"epoch {epoch}"):
        lossD, lossG, d_real = train_step(imgs)
        plot.log(lossD=lossD, lossG=lossG, D_real=d_real)                     # every step
        if plot.n % 250 == 0:
            ax_samples.imshow(netG(fixed_noise), rows=2, vmin=-1, vmax=1)     # replaces the last picture
plot.finish()
  • ax.plot("lossD", "lossG") names metrics. It takes no data. The values come from plot.log.
  • ax.twinx() is the panel's right-hand y-axis, as in matplotlib.
  • figsize is the size of the whole figure in inches. width_ratios and height_ratios are matplotlib's: width_ratios=(1, 1.25) gives the second column more room.
  • Other keyword arguments go to LivePlot, for example total or smooth. To wrap a single loop, pass iterable=loader.

The grid never grows. A metric that you log without placing it joins the first panel that is still empty, or the first curve panel if none is empty.

docs.title: What subplots returns
docs.text:
The second return value follows matplotlib's squeeze rules:

Grid axes is 1 x 1 one panel one row or one column a flat list of panels anything larger a 2-d grid: axes[0][1] and axes[0, 1] both work, and axes.flat lists every panel

squeeze=False always returns the 2-d grid.

docs.title: plot.imshow for a single picture
docs.text:
When you only need one picture, plot.imshow adds an image panel on first use. Every later call replaces the picture.

plot = LivePlot(range(steps))
for step in plot:
    plot.log(loss=train_step())
    if step % 100 == 0:
        plot.imshow(model(holdout))

On a plot made by subplots, call imshow on a panel instead.

docs.title: What imshow accepts
docs.text:
Torch tensors, numpy arrays and other array-likes. Tensors are detached and moved to the CPU for you. liveplot does not import torch.

Shape Read as (H, W), (1, H, W) one grayscale image (H, W, 3), (H, W, 4) one colour image, channels last (B, H, W) B grayscale images (B, 1|3|4, H, W) B images, channels first (torch's layout) (B, H, W, 1|3|4) B images, channels last

(3, H, W) and (4, H, W) could be one colour image or several grayscale ones, so they raise an error. Pass channels="first" for one colour image or channels="none" for a batch of grayscale images.

A 3-d array whose last dimension is 3 or 4 is read as one colour image. So a batch of grayscale images that are 3 or 4 pixels wide needs channels="none".

docs.title: Grids
docs.text:
A batch is tiled into a grid.

  • rows=2 or cols=5 fixes one dimension. The other is inferred.
  • griddim=(rows, cols) fixes both. Missing cells are left blank and extra images are dropped.
  • With none of these the grid is near-square and at most max_cols (8) wide.
  • Only the first max_images (64) images are shown, with a warning. Pass max_images=None to show all of them.
  • Images sit edge to edge. padding=2 puts 2 pixels of pad_value around each one.

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text:
By default, values are scaled so that the minimum of the batch is black and the maximum is white.

  • vmin and vmax fix the range. This is worth doing for a live view. Otherwise the brightness of the whole picture changes from frame to frame as the batch's range changes.
  • scale_each=True scales each image to its own range.
  • uint8 input is shown as it is, unless you give vmin or vmax.

vmin and vmax apply to colour images too. This differs from matplotlib's own imshow, which ignores them for colour data and clips floats to [0, 1]. A generator that ends in tanh outputs values in [-1, 1], so use vmin=-1, vmax=1.

docs.title: The step in the title
docs.text:
The title of an image panel shows the step at which the picture was drawn, for example "generator samples (step 250)". The picture only changes when you call imshow, so this tells you how old it is.

examples/dcgan_synthetic.py is a complete example on a fake DCGAN run.

docs.title: What log accepts
docs.text:
plot.log takes metric values by name:

plot.log(loss=0.3, acc=0.9)          # at the current x
plot.log(step, loss=0.3)             # at an explicit x
plot.log(step, {"loss": 0.3})        # a dict, useful when names are not valid Python identifiers
plot.log({"loss": 0.3})              # a dict at the current x

A value is anything float() accepts. That includes a one-element tensor. For a tensor that requires grad, PyTorch warns when it is converted, so pass loss.item() or loss.detach().

docs.title: Different rates need nothing special
docs.text:
Every metric keeps its own list of (x, value) points. Each log call adds a point to the metrics it names, at the current x. So a metric logged every step gets a point per step, and a metric logged every 50 steps gets a point every 50 steps. Both are drawn against the same x-axis.

plot = LivePlot(range(num_steps), "loss | eval_loss eval_acc")
for step in plot:
    plot.log(loss=train_step())                              # every step
    if step % 50 == 0:
        eval_loss, eval_acc = evaluate()
        plot.log(eval_loss=eval_loss, eval_acc=eval_acc)     # every 50 steps

docs.title: Once per epoch
docs.text:
Log after the inner loop. The point lands at the x the count has reached, which is the number of batches so far:

plot = LivePlot("loss", "acc")
for epoch in range(epochs):
    for batch in plot(loader, desc=f"epoch {epoch}"):
        plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))
    plot.log(acc=evaluate())      # at x = (epoch + 1) * len(loader)
plot.finish()

docs.title: Reading the values back
docs.text:
• plot.data is the full history: {metric: (xs, values)}, two lists per metric.
  • plot.latest is the most recent value of each metric.

Both are filled in whether or not anything is drawn, so they also work in a script.

xs, losses = plot.data["loss"]
best = min(losses)

docs.title: Collecting without drawing
docs.text: LivePlot(..., show=False) draws nothing. The metrics are still collected and the progress bar still shows the latest values. progress=False turns the bar off. The two options are independent.

docs.title: Panels and layout strings
docs.text: The figure is a grid of panels. Each panel holds one or more curves and has one or two y-axes.

docs.title: No layout: one shared panel
docs.text:
Metrics are created by logging them. With no layout, they all share one panel, with a legend:

plot = LivePlot(range(300))
for step in plot:
    plot.log(loss=..., val_loss=...)    # one panel, two curves

docs.title: Layout strings
docs.text:
Pass one string per panel, after the iterable if there is one:

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss", "return | entropy", "lossD lossG | acc")

Within a string:

  • Names separated by spaces share the left y-axis.
  • Names after a | go on a right-hand y-axis. A string can have at most one |.

So the example has three panels:

String Left axis Right axis "loss" loss none "return | entropy" return entropy "lossD lossG | acc" lossD, lossG acc

Metric names cannot contain spaces or | in a layout string.

docs.title: Common cases
docs.text:
Two metrics on one axis:

plot = LivePlot(loader, "train_loss val_loss")

A metric on the right-hand axis:

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss | acc")

Several panels:

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss", "acc", "lr")

docs.title: Metrics that no string mentions
docs.text:
With a layout, a metric you log that no string mentions gets a new panel of its own, added to the end of the grid:

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss")
...
plot.log(loss=0.3, lr=1e-3)     # lr gets its own panel

docs.title: What a panel shows by default
docs.text:
• The title is the metric names joined by " / ".
  • The x label is the plot's unit, "step" by default.
  • A panel with two y-axes labels each axis with its metric names. A panel with one y-axis has no y label.
  • Every panel has a legend. It lists the curves of both y-axes.

All of these can be changed. See Customising axes.

docs.title: The grid
docs.text:
Panels fill the grid row by row. By default the grid is at most three columns wide.

Option Effect max_cols Widest grid. The default is 3. None gives a near-square grid. rows Fix the number of rows. cols Fix the number of columns. cell_size (width, height) of one panel in inches. The default is (5, 3.5). dpi Resolution of the image. The default is 100. 
plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss", "acc", "lr", "grad_norm", cols=2, cell_size=(4, 3))

For a fixed grid that you fill panel by panel, as with plt.subplots, use LivePlot.subplots. See Images with subplots and imshow.

docs.title: The dict form
docs.text: A panel can also be given as a dict in place of a string, for example {"metrics": ["acc"], "ylim": (0, 1), "ylabel": "test accuracy"}. This form is older. The setters in Customising axes do the same job and are the intended way.

docs.title: Reference lines
docs.text: Reference lines mark a level a curve should reach, or a moment in the run. The method names are matplotlib's: axhline for a horizontal line and axvline for a vertical one.

docs.title: Horizontal lines
docs.text:
Call axhline on the axis of the metric the line belongs with:

plot["loss"].axhline(math.log(d_vocab), "uniform")       # the loss of a uniform guess
plot["return"].axhline(500, "solved", color="green")
  • The line is dashed grey by default. Extra keyword arguments (color, linestyle, linewidth, alpha) go to matplotlib.
  • The second argument is the label. It appears in the panel's legend. Without a label, the legend shows the number.
  • On a panel with two y-axes, the line uses the scale of the axis you called it on. plot["acc"].axhline(0.9) is drawn against the right-hand axis if acc is on the right.

plot.axhline(y, label) on the plot itself draws the line on the left axis of every panel that exists at that moment. Panels created later do not get it. plot.axhline(y, label, metric="loss") is the same as plot["loss"].axhline(y, label).

docs.title: Vertical lines
docs.text:
plot.axvline(label="lr drop")                   # every panel, at the current step
plot.panels[1].axvline(2000, "checkpoint")      # one panel, at x = 2000
  • Without an x, the line is drawn at the current step, plot.step, at the time of the call. So you can mark an event at the point in the loop where it happens.
  • The line is dotted grey by default. Extra keyword arguments go to matplotlib.
  • The label is written along the line. It does not appear in the legend.
  • plot.axvline draws on every panel that holds curves, including panels created later. Image panels are skipped.
for step in plot:
    if step == warmup_steps:
        plot.axvline(label="warmup ends")
    plot.log(loss=train_step())

docs.title: A matplotlib figure of the current state
docs.text:
plot.figure() returns a matplotlib Figure of the plot as it stands: the same panels, curves, reference lines and images.

fig = plot.figure()
fig.suptitle("run 12")
fig.savefig("run12.png", dpi=150)

The figure is built from plot.data when you call it. It is separate from the live display, so changing it does not change the live plot. It works during the run and after it, and also in a script or with show=False, where nothing is drawn live.

docs.title: Recording a GIF
docs.text:
record="run.gif" keeps every frame that is drawn and writes an animated GIF when the plot finishes:

plot = LivePlot(range(steps), "loss | acc", record="run.gif")
for step in plot:
    plot.log(loss=train_step())

The GIF replays at the pace of the run. Recording also works in a plain script, where nothing is displayed.

record=True keeps the frames without writing a file. Write one later with plot.save_gif:

plot = LivePlot(range(steps), record=True)
...
plot.save_gif("run.gif", speedup=2.0)     # twice as fast as the run

The frames are in plot.frames as (seconds since the plot was created, PNG bytes) pairs. plot.last_png is the most recent frame.

One frame is recorded per redraw, so refresh_seconds sets how many frames a recording has.

docs.title: Smoothing
docs.text:
Per-step losses are noisy. set_smooth draws a smoothed curve and keeps the raw values as a faded line behind it.

plot.set_smooth(0.9)                  # every panel
plot.panels[0].set_smooth(0.9)        # one panel
plot["loss"].set_smooth(0.9)          # the panel that holds loss
plot = LivePlot(loader, smooth=0.9)   # the default for every panel, set at creation
  • The weight is a number from 0 up to, but not including, 1. Larger is smoother. 0 turns smoothing off.
  • Smoothing belongs to a panel. All curves on the panel are smoothed, on both y-axes.
  • plot.data always holds the raw values. Smoothing only changes what is drawn.

The method is wandb's default, the time-weighted exponential moving average, with the same meaning of the weight as wandb's smoothing slider.

As in wandb, the amount of smoothing depends on how the points are spread over the x range of the plot, not on how many points there are. By default the x range is the range of the data so far, so a short run with few points is barely smoothed, and the smoothed curve can shift a little as the run grows. With fixed_x=True and a total, the x range is the whole run from the start.

docs.title: Log axes
docs.text:
plot["loss"].set_yscale("log")        # the axis that holds loss
plot.set_yscale("log")                # the left axis of every panel

The scale is "linear" or "log". Only the y-axis has a scale setting.

docs.title: x is a step counter
docs.text:
The plot keeps a counter of items consumed, plot.n, like tqdm's n. The x value of a logged point is

x = initial + n * unit_scale

at the time of the log call. With the defaults (initial=0, unit_scale=1) that is just n. The plot never looks at the items themselves.

n is 0 inside the loop body for the first item, like for step in range(N). It goes up by one after each item.

log does not change n. Something else has to.

docs.title: Wrap the loop
docs.text:
A single loop: pass the iterable to the constructor and iterate the plot.

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss")
for batch in plot:
    plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))

This shows one progress bar and finishes the plot when the loop ends.

Nested loops: create the plot once and wrap the inner loop with plot(...). The count continues from one epoch to the next. Each wrapped loop gets its own progress bar, and keyword arguments such as desc go to tqdm.

plot = LivePlot("loss", "acc")
for epoch in range(epochs):
    for batch in plot(loader, desc=f"epoch {epoch}"):
        plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))
    plot.log(acc=evaluate())
plot.finish()

If you already have a tqdm bar, pass it as the iterable. It is reused instead of wrapped in a second bar: LivePlot(tqdm(loader), "loss").

docs.title: Call update()
docs.text:
plot.update() advances the count by one, like tqdm's update. Use it when you do not want to wrap the loop. Call it after logging the step's metrics.

plot = LivePlot("loss", total=epochs * len(loader))
for epoch in range(epochs):
    plot.set_description(f"epoch {epoch}")
    for batch in loader:
        plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))
        plot.update()
plot.finish()

The first update() opens one progress bar for the whole run.

docs.title: Pass the step yourself
docs.text:
Give the x value as the first argument of log:

with LivePlot("loss") as plot:
    for step in range(num_steps):
        plot.log(step, loss=train_step())

Nothing is counted here and no progress bar is shown. The step can be any number, for example examples seen or seconds elapsed.

Inside a wrapped loop, an explicit step applies to that one log call. Without a wrapped loop, it also becomes the x of later log calls that give no step.

docs.title: What happens if you do none of these
docs.text:
Every point is logged at x = initial, which is 0 by default:

plot = LivePlot()
for batch in loader:
    plot.log(loss=train_step(batch))

plot.data["loss"][0]   # [0, 0, 0, ...]

The figure shows a vertical line.

docs.title: total and fixed_x
docs.text:
total is the number of items in the whole run. It is optional.

You write total is LivePlot(range(1000)), LivePlot(loader) taken from len() LivePlot("loss", total=epochs * len(loader)) what you gave LivePlot("loss") None

What it changes:

  • The progress bar, when the bar cannot get a length from what it wraps. That is the bar opened by plot.update(), and the bar for an iterable with no len(), such as a generator. With a total the bar shows a percentage and a time remaining. Without one it shows a plain count.
  • The x range, but only with fixed_x=True.

Bars made by plot(loader) use len(loader). They do not use total.

fixed_x is False by default: the x-axis grows with the data, and total does not change the figure. With fixed_x=True and a known total, the x-axis is fixed to

(initial, initial + total * unit_scale)

from the first frame, and the curve grows into it from the left.

plot = LivePlot(range(1000), "loss", fixed_x=True)                      # x-axis is 0 to 1000 throughout
plot = LivePlot("loss", total=epochs * len(loader), fixed_x=True)       # the same for nested loops

fixed_x=True without a total has no effect. To fix the x range of one panel by hand, use set_xlim.

docs.title: initial, unit and unit_scale
docs.text:
These are tqdm's arguments with tqdm's meaning.

  • initial is the x of the first item. Use initial=1 for a 1-based axis, or initial=10 to plot range(10, 20) at its own values.
  • unit names one item. It is the default x label and the unit on the progress bar. The default is "step".
  • unit_scale is how far x moves per item.

To plot against examples seen instead of batches:

plot = LivePlot(loader, "loss", unit="examples", unit_scale=batch_size)

The x values are then 0, batch_size, 2 * batch_size, and so on. The progress bar shows the same numbers.

docs.title: Reading the current x
docs.text: plot.step is the x that a log call would get right now. plot.n is the raw item count.
